Chapter 1 · Geography · Contemporary India II

Resources and Development

Everything we use comes from the environment — but only when technology, institutions and human effort turn it into a resource. This chapter looks at how resources are classified, why they must be planned and conserved, and how land and soil are used, degraded and saved in India.

Chapter Overview

What this chapter is about, at a glance

Everything available in our environment which can be used to satisfy our needs — provided it is technologically accessible, economically feasible and culturally acceptable — is called a resource. The transformation of things available in our environment involves an interactive relationship between nature, technology and institutions. Human beings interact with nature through technology and create institutions to accelerate their economic development.

Resources are not free gifts of nature. They are a function of human activities: human beings are themselves essential components of resources, because they transform material available in the environment into resources and use them.

The chapter then moves from the idea of a resource to development of resources (the problems of depletion, accumulation and ecological crisis), sustainable development, the Rio Earth Summit 1992 and Agenda 21, resource planning in India, and the conservation of resources.

The second half is about two specific resources — land and soil: land use categories, the land use pattern of India, land degradation and its conservation measures, the formation and classification of soils (alluvial, black, red and yellow, laterite, arid, forest), and finally soil erosion and soil conservation.

Classification of resources

On the basis of origin (biotic/abiotic), exhaustibility (renewable/non-renewable), ownership (individual, community, national, international) and status of development (potential, developed stock, reserves).

Three steps of resource planning

Identification and inventory; evolving a planning structure with technology, skill and institutions; matching resource plans with national development plans.

Land relief of India

Plains 43%, mountains 30%, plateaus 27% of the total surface area.

Land use data

Total geographical area 3.28 million sq km; land use data available for only 93% of it.

Forest cover target

33% of the geographical area, as outlined in the National Forest Policy (1952).

Six soil types

Alluvial, black (regur), red and yellow, laterite, arid, forest and mountainous.

Soil conservation methods

Contour ploughing, terrace cultivation, strip cropping, shelter belts.

Learning Objectives

What you should be able to do after studying

  • Explain what a resource is and why resources are a function of human activity, not free gifts of nature.
  • Classify resources on four bases — origin, exhaustibility, ownership and status of development — and give examples of each.
  • Describe the problems created by indiscriminate use of resources and explain the idea of sustainable development.
  • State what Agenda 21 is and why the Rio de Janeiro Earth Summit (1992) mattered.
  • Explain the three stages of resource planning and why India needs balanced planning at national, state, regional and local levels.
  • Name the thinkers, books and reports associated with resource conservation, with their years.
  • List the five land use categories and define net sown area and gross cropped area.
  • Read the land use pie charts of 1960–61 and 2019–20 and explain why the shares changed only marginally.
  • Identify the causes of land degradation in different states and the measures used to check it.
  • Describe the factors of soil formation and explain the six major soil types of India with their crops and regions.
  • Distinguish between bangar and khadar, and between gully, sheet and wind erosion.
  • Explain contour ploughing, terrace cultivation, strip cropping and shelter belts.

What is a Resource?
NCERT definition

Resource: Everything available in our environment which can be used to satisfy our needs, provided it is technologically accessible, economically feasible and culturally acceptable.

The process of transformation of things available in our environment involves an interactive relationship between nature, technology and institutions. Human beings interact with nature through technology and create institutions to accelerate their economic development.

NCERT text

Do you think that resources are free gifts of nature as is assumed by many? They are not. Resources are a function of human activities. Human beings themselves are essential components of resources. They transform material available in our environment into resources and use them.

Resources can be classified in the following ways:

  • On the basis of origin — biotic and abiotic
  • On the basis of exhaustibility — renewable and non-renewable
  • On the basis of ownership — individual, community, national and international
  • On the basis of status of development — potential, developed stock and reserves
Classification of resources with examples
BasisTypeMeaningExamples
OriginBioticObtained from the biosphere, i.e. living matterHuman beings, flora and fauna, fisheries, livestock
OriginAbioticNon-living thingsRocks, metals, minerals
ExhaustibilityRenewableCan be renewed or reproduced by physical, chemical or mechanical processesSolar and wind energy, water, forests, wildlife
ExhaustibilityNon-renewableTake millions of years to form and get exhaustedMinerals, fossil fuels (coal, petroleum, natural gas)
OwnershipIndividualOwned by private individualsPlot, house, farm, well
OwnershipCommunityAccessible to all members of a communityGrazing grounds, village ponds, public parks, burial grounds
OwnershipNationalAll resources within the political boundaries and territorial waters of a nationRoads, canals, railways, minerals
OwnershipInternationalRegulated by international institutionsOceanic areas beyond 200 nautical miles — the open ocean
Status of developmentPotentialFound in a region but not yet utilisedSolar and wind energy of Rajasthan and Gujarat; western parts of Gujarat have not been developed properly
Status of developmentDevelopedSurveyed, with quantity and quality determined for usePetroleum and natural gas in Bombay High, coal in the Ruhr region of Germany
Status of developmentStock / ReservesStock: materials in the environment that can satisfy needs but have no technology to use them (water in a pond, hydrogen in water). Reserves: a part of stock that can be used with existing technology, e.g. water in a dam.

Development of Resources

Resources are vital for human survival as well as for maintaining the quality of life. It was believed that resources are free gifts of nature. As a result, human beings used them indiscriminately and this has led to the following major problems:

  • Depletion of resources for satisfying the greed of a few individuals.
  • Accumulation of resources in few hands, which, in turn, divided the society into two segments, i.e. haves and have-nots, or rich and poor.
  • Indiscriminate exploitation of resources has led to global ecological crises such as global warming, ozone layer depletion, environmental pollution and land degradation.

An equitable distribution of resources has become essential for a sustained quality of life and global peace. If the present trend of resource depletion by a few individuals and countries continues, the future of our planet is in danger. Therefore, resource planning is essential for sustainable existence of all forms of life. Sustainable existence is a component of sustainable development.

NCERT definition

Sustainable economic development means development should take place without damaging the environment, and development in the present should not compromise with the needs of the future generations.

Teacher explanation

Why this matters: the sentence “development in the present should not compromise with the needs of the future generations” is the definition most often asked in exams. Learn it word for word, and remember that “sustainable existence” is described in the chapter as a component of sustainable development.

Rio de Janeiro Earth Summit, 1992 and Agenda 21

In June 1992, more than 100 heads of states met in Rio de Janeiro in Brazil, for the first International Earth Summit. The Summit was convened for addressing urgent problems of environmental protection and socio-economic development at the global level. The assembled leaders signed the Declaration on Global Climatic Change and Biological Diversity. The Rio Convention endorsed the global Forest Principles and adopted Agenda 21 for achieving sustainable development in the 21st century.

Agenda 21

Agenda 21 is the declaration signed by world leaders in 1992 at the United Nations Conference on Environment and Development (UNCED), which took place at Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. It aims at achieving global sustainable development. It is an agenda to combat environmental damage, poverty and disease through global co-operation on common interests, mutual needs and shared responsibilities. One major objective of Agenda 21 is that every local government should draw its own local Agenda 21.

Resource Planning

Planning is the widely accepted strategy for judicious use of resources. It has importance in a country like India, which has enormous diversity in the availability of resources. There are regions which are rich in certain types of resources but are deficient in some other resources. There are some regions which can be considered self-sufficient in terms of the availability of resources, and there are some regions which have acute shortage of some vital resources.

Regional resource differences given in the chapter
RegionRich inDeficient in
Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Madhya PradeshMinerals and coal deposits—
Arunachal PradeshAbundance of water resourcesInfrastructural development
RajasthanSolar and wind energyWater resources
Ladakh (cold desert)Very rich cultural heritage; relatively isolated from the rest of the countryWater, infrastructure and some vital minerals

This calls for balanced resource planning at the national, state, regional and local levels.

Resource planning in India

Resource planning is a complex process which involves:

  1. Identification and inventory of resources across the regions of the country. This involves surveying, mapping and qualitative and quantitative estimation and measurement of the resources.
  2. Evolving a planning structure endowed with appropriate technology, skill and institutional set-up for implementing resource development plans.
  3. Matching the resource development plans with overall national development plans.

India has made concerted efforts for achieving the goals of resource planning right from the First Five Year Plan launched after Independence.

Why resources alone are not enough

The availability of resources is a necessary condition for the development of any region, but mere availability of resources in the absence of corresponding changes in technology and institutions may hinder development. There are many regions in our country that are rich in resources but these are included in economically backward regions. On the contrary, there are some regions which have a poor resource base but they are economically developed.

The history of colonisation reveals that rich resources in colonies were the main attraction for foreign invaders. It was primarily the higher level of technological development of the colonising countries that helped them to exploit resources of other regions and establish their supremacy over the colonies. Therefore, resources can contribute to development only when they are accompanied by appropriate technological development and institutional changes. India has experienced all this in different phases of colonisation. Hence in India, development in general, and resource development in particular, does not only involve the availability of resources but also technology, the quality of human resources and the historical experiences of the people.

Do it yourself

Can you name some resource-rich but economically backward regions and some resource-poor but economically developed regions? Give reasons for such a situation.

Activity

What resources are being developed in your surroundings by the community/village panchayats/ward-level communities with the help of community participation? Prepare a list of resources found in your state and also identify the resources that are important but deficient in your state.

Conservation of Resources

Resources are vital for any developmental activity. But irrational consumption and over-utilisation of resources may lead to socio-economic and environmental problems. To overcome these problems, resource conservation at various levels is important. This had been the main concern of leaders and thinkers in the past.

“There is enough for everybody’s need and not for anybody’s greed.”

— Mahatma Gandhi

Gandhiji placed the greedy and selfish individuals and the exploitative nature of modern technology as the root cause for resource depletion at the global level. He was against mass production and wanted to replace it with production by the masses.

First systematic international advocacy of resource conservation.

Land Resources

We live on land, we perform our economic activities on land and we use it in different ways. Thus, land is a natural resource of utmost importance. It supports natural vegetation, wildlife, human life, economic activities, transport and communication systems. However, land is an asset of a finite magnitude; therefore, it is important to use it for various purposes with careful planning.

India has land under a variety of relief features, namely mountains, plateaus, plains and islands.

Land under important relief features (Fig. 1.3)
Relief featureShare of total surface areaWhat it provides
PlainsAbout 43%Facilities for agriculture and industry
Mountains30%Ensure perennial flow of some rivers; provide facilities for tourism and ecological aspects
PlateausAbout 27%Rich reserves of minerals, fossil fuels and forests
Land Utilisation

Land resources are used for the following purposes:

  1. Forests
  2. Land not available for cultivation — (a) barren and waste land; (b) land put to non-agricultural uses, e.g. buildings, roads, factories.
  3. Other uncultivated land (excluding fallow land) — (a) permanent pastures and grazing land; (b) land under miscellaneous tree crops and groves (not included in net sown area); (c) culturable waste land (left uncultivated for more than five agricultural years).
  4. Fallow lands — (a) current fallow (left without cultivation for one or less than one agricultural year); (b) other than current fallow (left uncultivated for the past one to five agricultural years).
  5. Net sown area — the physical extent of land on which crops are sown and harvested.
Definition

Gross cropped area = area sown more than once in an agricultural year + net sown area.

Teacher explanation

Remember the difference: net sown area counts land once; gross cropped area counts the same land again if a second crop is grown on it. So gross cropped area is always equal to or larger than net sown area.

Land Use Pattern in India

The use of land is determined both by physical factors such as topography, climate and soil types, as well as human factors such as population density, technological capability, and culture and traditions.

The total geographical area of India is 3.28 million sq km. Land use data, however, is available only for 93 per cent of the total geographical area, because the land use reporting for most of the north-east states except Assam has not been done fully. Moreover, some areas of Jammu and Kashmir occupied by Pakistan and China have also not been surveyed.

Land use categories, 2019–20 (reporting area = 100 per cent)
CategoryShare
Net sown area45.64%
Forest23.41%
Barren and unculturable waste land5.40%
Area under non-agricultural uses9.06%
Permanent pasture and grazing land3.42%
Area under miscellaneous tree crops and groves1.02%
Culturable waste land3.90%
Fallow other than current fallow3.67%
Current fallow4.49%

The land under permanent pasture has also decreased. Most of the land other than current fallow is either of poor quality or the cost of cultivation of such land is very high. Hence these lands are cultivated once or twice in about two to three years; if these are included in the net sown area, then the percentage of net sown area in India comes to about 54 per cent of the total reporting area.

The pattern of net sown area varies greatly from one state to another. It is over 80 per cent of the total area in Punjab and Haryana and less than 10 per cent in Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram, Manipur and Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

Forest area in the country is far lower than the desired 33 per cent of the geographical area, as it was outlined in the National Forest Policy (1952). It was considered essential for the maintenance of the ecological balance. The livelihood of millions of people who live on the fringes of these forests depends upon it. A part of the land is termed as waste land, and land put to other non-agricultural uses. Waste land includes rocky, arid and desert areas; land put to other non-agricultural uses includes settlements, roads, railways and industry.

Continuous use of land over a long period of time without taking appropriate measures to conserve and manage it has resulted in land degradation. This, in turn, has serious repercussions on society and the environment.

Land Degradation and Conservation Measures

We have shared our land with past generations and will have to do so with future generations too. Ninety-five per cent of our basic needs for food, shelter and clothing are obtained from land. Human activities have not only brought about degradation of land but have also aggravated the pace of natural forces to cause damage to land.

Some human activities such as deforestation, overgrazing, mining and quarrying too have contributed significantly to land degradation.

Causes of land degradation and the states affected (as given in the chapter)
CauseStates mentionedHow it degrades land
Deforestation due to miningJharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, OdishaMining sites are abandoned after excavation, leaving deep scars and traces of over-burdening.
OvergrazingGujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, MaharashtraOne of the main reasons for land degradation in these states.
Over-irrigationPunjab, Haryana, western Uttar PradeshWater logging leads to increase in salinity and alkalinity in the soil.
Mineral processing (grinding of limestone for cement, calcite and soapstone for ceramic)—Generates huge quantities of dust in the atmosphere; when it settles it retards the infiltration of water into the soil.
Industrial effluents as wasteMany parts of the countryIn recent years a major source of land and water pollution.

Ways to solve the problems of land degradation

  • Afforestation and proper management of grazing can help to some extent.
  • Planting of shelter belts of plants, control on overgrazing and stabilisation of sand dunes by growing thorny bushes are methods to check land degradation in arid areas.
  • Proper management of waste lands, control of mining activities, proper discharge and disposal of industrial effluents and wastes after treatment can reduce land and water degradation in industrial and suburban areas.
Soil as a Resource

Soil is the most important natural resource. It is the medium of plant growth and supports different types of living organisms on the earth. The soil is a living system. It takes millions of years to form soil up to a few centimetres in depth.

Relief, parent rock or bedrock, climate, vegetation and other forms of life, and time are important factors in the formation of soil. Various forces of nature such as change in temperature, actions of running water, wind and glaciers, activities of decomposers, etc., contribute to the formation of soil. Chemical and organic changes which take place in the soil are equally important. Soil also consists of organic (humus) and inorganic materials.

On the basis of the factors responsible for soil formation, colour, thickness, texture, age, and chemical and physical properties, the soils of India are classified into different types.

Classification of Soils

India has varied relief features, landforms, climatic realms and vegetation types. These have contributed to the development of various types of soils.

Alluvial Soils

This is the most widely spread and important soil. In fact, the entire northern plains are made of alluvial soil. These have been deposited by three important Himalayan river systems — the Indus, the Ganga and the Brahmaputra. These soils also extend in Rajasthan and Gujarat through a narrow corridor. Alluvial soil is also found in the eastern coastal plains, particularly in the deltas of the Mahanadi, the Godavari, the Krishna and the Kaveri rivers.

The alluvial soil consists of various proportions of sand, silt and clay. As we move inland towards the river valleys, soil particles appear somewhat bigger in size. In the upper reaches of the river valley, i.e. near the place of the break of slope, the soils are coarse. Such soils are more common in piedmont plains such as Duars, Chos and Terai.

According to their age, alluvial soils can be classified as old alluvial (Bangar) and new alluvial (Khadar). The bangar soil has a higher concentration of kanker nodules than the khadar. It has more fine particles and is more fertile than the bangar. Alluvial soils as a whole are very fertile.

Mostly these soils contain adequate proportions of potash, phosphoric acid and lime, which are ideal for the growth of sugarcane, paddy, wheat and other cereal and pulse crops. Due to their high fertility, regions of alluvial soils are intensively cultivated and densely populated. Soils in the drier areas are more alkaline and can be productive after proper treatment and irrigation.

Black Soil

These soils are black in colour and are also known as regur soils. Black soil is ideal for growing cotton and is also known as black cotton soil. It is believed that climatic conditions along with the parent rock material are the important factors for the formation of black soil. This type of soil is typical of the Deccan trap (Basalt) region spread over the north-west Deccan plateau and is made up of lava flows.

They cover the plateaus of Maharashtra, Saurashtra, Malwa, Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh and extend in the south-east direction along the Godavari and Krishna valleys.

The black soils are made up of extremely fine, i.e. clayey material. They are well known for their capacity to hold moisture. In addition, they are rich in soil nutrients such as calcium carbonate, magnesium, potash and lime. These soils are generally poor in phosphoric contents. They develop deep cracks during hot weather, which helps in the proper aeration of the soil. These soils are sticky when wet and difficult to work on unless tilled immediately after the first shower or during the pre-monsoon period.

Red and Yellow Soils

Red soil develops on crystalline igneous rocks in areas of low rainfall in the eastern and southern parts of the Deccan plateau. Yellow and red soils are also found in parts of Odisha, Chhattisgarh, southern parts of the middle Ganga plain and along the piedmont zone of the Western Ghats. These soils develop a reddish colour due to the diffusion of iron in crystalline and metamorphic rocks. It looks yellow when it occurs in a hydrated form.

Laterite Soil

Laterite has been derived from the Latin word “later”, which means brick. The laterite soil develops under tropical and subtropical climates with alternate wet and dry seasons. This soil is the result of intense leaching due to heavy rain.

Lateritic soils are mostly deep to very deep, acidic (pH < 6.0), generally deficient in plant nutrients, and occur mostly in the southern states, the Western Ghats region of Maharashtra, Odisha, some parts of West Bengal and the north-east regions. Where these soils support deciduous and evergreen forests, they are humus rich, but under sparse vegetation and in a semi-arid environment they are generally humus poor. They are prone to erosion and degradation due to their position on the landscape.

After adopting appropriate soil conservation techniques, particularly in the hilly areas of Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu, this soil is very useful for growing tea and coffee. Red laterite soils in Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and Kerala are more suitable for crops like cashew nut.

Arid Soils

Arid soils range from red to brown in colour. They are generally sandy in texture and saline in nature. In some areas the salt content is very high and common salt is obtained by evaporating the water. Due to the dry climate and high temperature, evaporation is faster and the soil lacks humus and moisture.

The lower horizons of the soil are occupied by kankar because of the increasing calcium content downwards. The kankar layer formations in the bottom horizons restrict the infiltration of water. After proper irrigation these soils become cultivable, as has been the case in western Rajasthan.

Forest Soils

These soils are found in the hilly and mountainous areas where sufficient rain forests are available. The soil texture varies according to the mountain environment where they are formed. They are loamy and silty in valley sides and coarse grained in the upper slopes. In the snow-covered areas of the Himalayas, these soils experience denudation and are acidic with low humus content. The soils found in the lower parts of the valleys, particularly on the river terraces and alluvial fans, are fertile.

Soil Erosion and Soil Conservation

The denudation of the soil cover and subsequent washing down is described as soil erosion. The processes of soil formation and erosion go on simultaneously and generally there is a balance between the two. Sometimes this balance is disturbed due to human activities like deforestation, overgrazing, construction and mining, while natural forces like wind, glacier and water lead to soil erosion.

The running water cuts through the clayey soils and makes deep channels as gullies. The land becomes unfit for cultivation and is known as bad land. In the Chambal basin such lands are called ravines. Sometimes water flows as a sheet over large areas down a slope; in such cases the top soil is washed away. This is known as sheet erosion. Wind blows loose soil off flat or sloping land, which is known as wind erosion.

Soil erosion is also caused by defective methods of farming. Ploughing in a wrong way, i.e. up and down the slope, forms channels for the quick flow of water, leading to soil erosion.

Soil conservation methods
MethodHow it works
Contour ploughingPloughing along the contour lines can decelerate the flow of water down the slopes.
Terrace cultivationSteps can be cut out on the slopes making terraces; this restricts erosion. The western and central Himalayas have well-developed terrace farming.
Strip croppingLarge fields can be divided into strips, and strips of grass are left to grow between the crops. This breaks up the force of the wind.
Shelter beltsPlanting lines of trees to create shelter works in a similar way. Rows of such trees are called shelter belts. These have contributed significantly to the stabilisation of sand dunes and in stabilising the desert in western India.

Flashcards

All key terms

Key terms and definitions
TermSimple explanation
ResourceEverything available in our environment which can be used to satisfy our needs, provided it is technologically accessible, economically feasible and culturally acceptable.
Biotic resourceA resource obtained from the biosphere, i.e. living matter — human beings, flora and fauna, fisheries, livestock.
Abiotic resourceA non-living resource — rocks, metals and minerals.
Renewable resourceA resource that can be renewed or reproduced by physical, chemical or mechanical processes — solar and wind energy, water, forests, wildlife.
Non-renewable resourceA resource that takes millions of years to form and gets exhausted with use — minerals and fossil fuels.
Individual resourceA resource owned by a private individual, e.g. a plot, house, farm or well.
Community resourceA resource accessible to all members of a community — grazing grounds, village ponds, public parks, burial grounds.
National resourceAll resources within the political boundaries and territorial waters of a nation — roads, canals, railways, minerals.
International resourceResources regulated by international institutions, e.g. oceanic areas beyond 200 nautical miles.
Potential resourceA resource found in a region but not yet utilised, e.g. solar and wind energy in Rajasthan and Gujarat.
Developed resourceA resource that has been surveyed and whose quantity and quality have been determined for use, e.g. petroleum in Bombay High.
StockMaterials in our environment which can satisfy human needs but for which we do not have the appropriate technology to access them, e.g. water in a pond, hydrogen in water.
ReservesA part of the stock which can be put into use with the help of existing technical know-how, e.g. water in a dam.
Sustainable developmentDevelopment that takes place without damaging the environment, and development in the present that does not compromise the needs of future generations.
Agenda 21The declaration signed by world leaders in 1992 at UNCED, Rio de Janeiro, to achieve global sustainable development; it asks every local government to draw its own local Agenda 21.
Resource planningJudicious use of resources through identification and inventory, a planning structure with technology and institutions, and matching with national development plans.
Net sown areaThe physical extent of land on which crops are sown and harvested.
Gross cropped areaArea sown more than once in an agricultural year plus net sown area.
Current fallowLand left without cultivation for one or less than one agricultural year.
Culturable waste landLand left uncultivated for more than five agricultural years.
Land degradationThe decline in land quality caused by continuous use without conservation — through deforestation, overgrazing, mining, over-irrigation and industrial waste.
HumusOrganic material in the soil formed from decomposed plant and animal matter; it makes soil fertile.
BangarOld alluvial soil; it has a higher concentration of kanker nodules and more fine particles.
KhadarNew alluvial soil; it is more fertile than bangar.
Regur soilBlack soil, formed from lava flows of the Deccan trap; ideal for cotton.
LateriteFrom the Latin word “later”, meaning brick — soil formed by intense leaching under alternate wet and dry seasons.
KankarCalcium carbonate nodules that form in the lower horizons of arid soils and restrict infiltration of water.
Soil erosionDenudation of the soil cover and its subsequent washing down.
Gully erosion / bad landDeep channels cut by running water in clayey soil; such land is unfit for cultivation. In the Chambal basin it is called ravines.
Sheet erosionWashing away of the top soil when water flows as a sheet over a large area down a slope.
Contour ploughingPloughing along contour lines to slow the flow of water down slopes.
Strip croppingDividing large fields into strips with strips of grass between crops to break the force of the wind.
Shelter beltsRows of trees planted to create shelter; they stabilise sand dunes and the desert in western India.

1968Club of Rome advocated resource conservation systematically
1974Schumacher’s Small is Beautiful restated Gandhian philosophy
1987Brundtland Commission Report introduced “sustainable development”; later published as Our Common Future
June 1992First International Earth Summit, Rio de Janeiro — Declaration on Global Climatic Change and Biological Diversity, global Forest Principles, Agenda 21
1960–61 and 2019–20The two years compared in the land use pie charts (Fig. 1.4)

Numbers and figures

  • 3.28 million sq km — total geographical area of India.
  • 93 per cent — share of the geographical area for which land use data is available.
  • 43% plains, 30% mountains, 27% plateaus — land under important relief features.
  • 45.64% — net sown area, 2019–20; about 54% if fallow land other than current fallow is included.
  • 23.41% — land under forest in 2019–20 (against a desired 33%).
  • Over 80% — net sown area in Punjab and Haryana; less than 10% in Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram, Manipur and Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
  • 95 per cent — share of basic needs for food, shelter and clothing obtained from land.
  • 33 per cent — forest area desired by the National Forest Policy, 1952.
  • pH < 6.0 — laterite soils are acidic.
  • Magnetite-like precision is not needed here: only the figures above appear in this chapter — do not add outside statistics to answers.

People, books and institutions

Who said or wrote what
NameContribution
Mahatma Gandhi“There is enough for everybody’s need and not for anybody’s greed.” Opposed mass production; wanted production by the masses.
Club of RomeAdvocated resource conservation for the first time in a more systematic way (1968).
SchumacherSmall is Beautiful (1974) — presented Gandhian philosophy again.
Brundtland CommissionReport of 1987 that introduced the concept of sustainable development; published as Our Common Future.
UNCED / Earth SummitRio de Janeiro, June 1992 — Agenda 21.

Regional examples you must be able to quote

  • Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh — rich in minerals and coal deposits.
  • Arunachal Pradesh — abundant water resources but lacks infrastructural development.
  • Rajasthan — endowed with solar and wind energy but lacks water resources.
  • Ladakh — rich cultural heritage, but deficient in water, infrastructure and some vital minerals.
  • Punjab, Haryana, western Uttar Pradesh — over-irrigation causes water logging, salinity and alkalinity.
  • Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra — overgrazing is a main cause of land degradation.
  • Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha — deforestation due to mining.
  • Duars, Chos and Terai — piedmont plains with coarse alluvial soils.
  • Chambal basin — ravines (bad land).
  • Western and central Himalayas — well-developed terrace farming.
  • Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu — laterite soil useful for tea and coffee after conservation.
  • Western Rajasthan — arid soils made cultivable after irrigation.
  • Neyveli (Tamil Nadu) appears in the minerals chapter, not here — do not mix chapters.

How to read the pie charts: each chart shows the share of the reporting area in one year. Compare the same slice across the two charts. Net sown area rose only from 45.26% to 45.64% and forest from 18.11% to 23.41%, which is why the chapter says the change is marginal. Non-agricultural use doubled, and barren land and culturable waste fell — land moved from waste categories into non-agricultural use.

07

NCERT In-text Questions and Answers

The questions printed inside the chapter

These are the “Can you…” and activity questions that appear inside the chapter text. Model answers are based on the chapter itself.

1.

Do you think that resources are free gifts of nature as is assumed by many?

Model answer

No. Resources are not free gifts of nature; they are a function of human activities. Human beings themselves are essential components of resources — they transform material available in the environment into resources and use them. A thing becomes a resource only when it is technologically accessible, economically feasible and culturally acceptable.

2.

Can you identify and name the various items used in making life comfortable in our villages and towns? List the items and name the material used in making them.

Model answer

For example: utensils (steel, aluminium), furniture (wood), clothes (cotton, silk), houses (bricks, cement, steel), vehicles (iron, aluminium, rubber), wires (copper), glassware (silica sand). Each item is made from material drawn from nature and processed with technology.

3.

Can you name some resource-rich but economically backward regions and some resource-poor but economically developed regions? Give reasons for such a situation.

Model answer

Resource-rich but backward: Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and Odisha have minerals and coal but limited industry and infrastructure. Resource-poor but developed: regions such as Punjab and Haryana have a modest mineral base but are agriculturally and industrially developed. The reason is that resources contribute to development only when accompanied by appropriate technology, institutional change, quality of human resources and historical experience — mere availability is not enough.

4.

What resources are being developed in your surroundings by the community/village panchayat/ward-level communities with community participation? Prepare a list of resources found in your state and also identify the resources that are important but deficit in your state.

Model answer

Answers vary by region. Typical examples of community-managed resources: village ponds and tanks, grazing land, community forests, rainwater harvesting structures, common water taps and wells, waste collection and segregation. A state list usually names land, water, forests, minerals and solar energy as available, and marks water, electricity or fodder as deficit. (Student answers may vary.)

5.

Find out the reasons for the low proportion of net sown area in Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram, Manipur and Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

Model answer

These are hilly, forested regions with steep slopes, heavy rainfall, dense forests and difficult terrain, so only a small part of the area can be cultivated. Shifting cultivation (jhumming) also leaves land fallow for long periods, and much of the land is under forest. Hence net sown area is less than 10 per cent.

6.

Try to do a comparison between the two pie charts (Fig. 1.4) given for land use and find out why the net sown area and the land under forests have changed from 1960–61 to 2019–20 very marginally.

Model answer

Net sown area moved only from 45.26% to 45.64% and forest from 18.11% to 23.41%. Land is a finite resource: the area that can be cultivated is limited by relief, soil and water, and much of the remaining land is either already built upon or too poor to cultivate. Forest land competes with agriculture, settlements and industry, so it has not reached the desired 33 per cent. Marginal change is therefore the result of a fixed land area and competing uses.

7.

The land under permanent pasture has also decreased. How are we able to feed our huge cattle population on this pasture land and what are the consequences of it?

Model answer

Permanent pasture fell from 4.71% to 3.42%. Cattle are increasingly fed on crop residues, fodder crops, stalks and grazing on fallow and forest land. The consequences are overgrazing on the remaining land, land degradation, lower milk and draught-animal productivity, and conflict over grazing land.

8.

Imagine, if the oil supply gets exhausted one day, how would this affect our lifestyle?

Model answer

Transport would be badly hit — buses, trucks, cars, trains and aircraft depend on oil. Prices of food and goods would rise because movement becomes costly. Industry using petroleum as fuel and raw material (plastics, fertilisers, synthetic fibres) would slow down. We would have to shift to public transport, electric vehicles, cycling and renewable energy, and to more local production and consumption.

08

NCERT Exercise Questions and Answers

End-of-chapter exercises, projects and activities

NCERT Exercises

Reproduced from the exercise section of the chapter, with model answers. Word limits are the ones the textbook sets.

1.
NCERT exercise1 mark

Multiple choice — Which one of the following is the main cause of land degradation in Punjab? (a) Intensive cultivation (b) Deforestation (c) Over-irrigation (d) Overgrazing

Model answer

(c) Over-irrigation. In Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh over-irrigation causes water logging, which increases salinity and alkalinity in the soil.

2.
NCERT exercise1 mark

Multiple choice — In which one of the following states is terrace cultivation practised? (a) Punjab (b) Plains of Uttar Pradesh (c) Haryana (d) Uttarakhand

Model answer

(d) Uttarakhand. Terrace cultivation is practised on slopes; the western and central Himalayas have well-developed terrace farming.

3.
NCERT exercise1 mark

Multiple choice — In which of the following states is black soil predominantly found? (a) Uttar Pradesh (b) Maharashtra (c) Rajasthan (d) Jharkhand

Model answer

(b) Maharashtra. Black (regur) soil covers the plateaus of Maharashtra, Saurashtra, Malwa, Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh.

4.
NCERT exercise2 marks

Name three states having black soil and the crop which is mainly grown in it. (about 30 words)

Model answer

Black soil is found in Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh (also Gujarat’s Saurashtra and Malwa). It is ideal for growing cotton, which is why it is called black cotton soil.

5.
NCERT exercise3 marks

What type of soil is found in the river deltas of the eastern coast? Give three main features of this type of soil. (about 30 words)

Model answer

Alluvial soil. Features: (i) it is very fertile and rich in potash, phosphoric acid and lime; (ii) it consists of various proportions of sand, silt and clay; (iii) it supports intensive cultivation of paddy, sugarcane and pulses and is found as khadar (new) and bangar (old).

6.
NCERT exercise3 marks

What steps can be taken to control soil erosion in the hilly areas? (about 30 words)

Model answer

Contour ploughing along contour lines, terrace cultivation by cutting steps on slopes, strip cropping, and planting shelter belts of trees. Contour ploughing and terracing slow the flow of water down slopes.

7.
NCERT exercise5 marks

Explain land use pattern in India and why the land under forest has not increased much since 1960–61. (about 120 words)

Model answer

India’s total geographical area is 3.28 million sq km, but land use data is available for only 93 per cent of it because reporting is incomplete in most north-east states except Assam and some areas of Jammu and Kashmir occupied by Pakistan and China have not been surveyed. Of the reporting area, net sown area is 45.64 per cent and forest 23.41 per cent (2019–20). Land not available for cultivation, other uncultivated land, fallow land and net sown area make up the rest. Forest has not increased much because land is finite and is under heavy pressure from a growing population: agricultural land cannot easily be spared, and settlements, roads, industry and infrastructure keep taking land. The 33 per cent target of the National Forest Policy (1952) has therefore not been reached, and only marginal change is visible between 1960–61 and 2019–20.

8.
NCERT exercise5 marks

How have technical and economic development led to more consumption of resources? (about 120 words)

Model answer

Technical development gives us machines, irrigation, transport, mining equipment and industry that can extract and process far more material than before, so resources that were once inaccessible become usable — but at a much faster rate. Economic development raises incomes and changes lifestyles: people buy more goods, travel more, live in larger houses and use more energy, so demand multiplies. Improved medical facilities and better food supply lower death rates, and population growth adds further demand. Technology also makes possible the exploitation of low-grade ores and distant resources, encouraging still more consumption. Since many of these resources are non-renewable and take millions of years to form, faster consumption means faster depletion, along with pollution and ecological crisis — which is why resource planning and conservation are needed.

9.
NCERT projectProject

Project/Activity — Make a project showing consumption and conservation of resources in your locality.

Model answer

Suggested plan: (i) list the resources used in your locality — water, electricity, fuel, food, building material; (ii) record how each is used and wasted over a week; (iii) draw a chart of consumption; (iv) suggest conservation steps such as rainwater harvesting, LED bulbs, waste segregation, public transport and tree planting; (v) show savings after a fortnight. (Student projects will vary.)

10.
NCERT projectProject

Project/Activity — Have a discussion in the class on how to conserve various resources used in your school.

Model answer

Points that usually come up: switching off fans and lights in empty classrooms; repairing leaking taps and using taps with aerators; rainwater harvesting on the school roof; paper recycling and both-side printing; a school kitchen garden; segregated dustbins; collecting and reusing old books; planting and caring for trees on campus. (Student answers may vary.)

11.
NCERT activityActivity

Project/Activity — Solve the word puzzle: (i) natural endowments in the form of land, water, vegetation and minerals; (ii) a type of non-renewable resource; (iii) soil with high water-retaining capacity; (iv) intensively leached soils of the monsoon climate; (v) plantation of trees on a large scale to check soil erosion; (vi) the Great Plains of India are made up of these soils.

Model answer

(i) RESOURCES (ii) MINERALS (iii) BLACK (soil) (iv) LATERITE (v) AFFORESTATION (vi) ALLUVIAL.

09

Important Questions and Answers

Board-style practice

Practice questions

Written in the style of CBSE board papers. They are additional practice, not NCERT originals.

1.

Define a resource. Why are resources considered a function of human activities? (2 marks)

Model answer

Everything available in our environment which can be used to satisfy our needs, provided it is technologically accessible, economically feasible and culturally acceptable, is a resource. Resources are a function of human activities because human beings transform material available in the environment into resources and use them; without technology, institutions and human effort, a substance in nature remains merely a substance.

2.

Explain the four bases on which resources are classified, with one example of each type. (5 marks)

Model answer

(i) Origin — biotic (flora, fauna, livestock) and abiotic (rocks, metals). (ii) Exhaustibility — renewable (solar, wind, water, forests) and non-renewable (minerals, fossil fuels). (iii) Ownership — individual (plot, house), community (grazing ground, pond), national (roads, railways, minerals) and international (oceanic areas beyond 200 nautical miles). (iv) Status of development — potential (solar energy of Rajasthan), developed (petroleum in Bombay High) and stock/reserves (water in a pond is stock; water in a dam is a reserve).

3.

Distinguish between stock and reserves. (2 marks)

Model answer

Stock are materials in our environment which can satisfy human needs but for which we do not have the appropriate technology to access them — for example water in a pond, or hydrogen in water. Reserves are that part of the stock which can be put into use with existing technical know-how — for example water in a dam.

4.

What problems arise from the indiscriminate use of resources? (3 marks)

Model answer

(i) Depletion of resources for satisfying the greed of a few individuals; (ii) accumulation of resources in few hands, dividing society into haves and have-nots; (iii) indiscriminate exploitation leading to global ecological crises such as global warming, ozone layer depletion, environmental pollution and land degradation.

5.

What is Agenda 21? Why is it called Agenda 21? (3 marks)

Model answer

Agenda 21 is the declaration signed by world leaders in 1992 at the United Nations Conference on Environment and Development (UNCED) held at Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. It aims at achieving global sustainable development by combating environmental damage, poverty and disease through global cooperation on common interests, mutual needs and shared responsibilities. Its major objective is that every local government should draw its own local Agenda 21.

6.

Explain the three steps involved in resource planning in India. (3 marks)

Model answer

(i) Identification and inventory of resources across the regions of the country, involving surveying, mapping and qualitative and quantitative estimation and measurement; (ii) evolving a planning structure endowed with appropriate technology, skill and institutional set-up for implementing resource development plans; (iii) matching resource development plans with overall national development plans.

7.

“Mere availability of resources is not enough for development.” Justify with examples. (5 marks)

Model answer

Many resource-rich regions are economically backward while some resource-poor regions are developed. Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and Madhya Pradesh have minerals and coal but remain less developed, while regions with a poor resource base have developed through technology and institutions. The history of colonisation shows that rich resources in colonies attracted invaders, and the higher technological development of colonising countries allowed them to exploit those resources. Hence resources contribute to development only when accompanied by appropriate technological development, institutional change, quality of human resources and historical experience.

8.

Describe the land use pattern of India. (5 marks)

Model answer

Land is used for forests; land not available for cultivation (barren and waste land, and land put to non-agricultural uses such as buildings, roads and factories); other uncultivated land excluding fallow (permanent pastures and grazing land, land under miscellaneous tree crops and groves, culturable waste land); fallow lands (current fallow and other than current fallow); and net sown area. In 2019–20, net sown area was 45.64% and forest 23.41% of the reporting area. Land use is determined by physical factors (topography, climate, soil) and human factors (population density, technology, culture and traditions).

9.

What is land degradation? Explain any four causes with the states affected. (5 marks)

Model answer

Land degradation is the decline in the quality and productivity of land due to continuous use without conservation. Causes: (i) deforestation due to mining in Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh and Odisha — abandoned mines leave deep scars and over-burden; (ii) overgrazing in Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra; (iii) over-irrigation in Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh causing water logging, salinity and alkalinity; (iv) mineral processing — grinding of limestone for cement and calcite and soapstone for ceramics — produces dust that settles on land and retards infiltration of water; (v) industrial effluents, now a major source of land and water pollution.

10.

Describe the measures for land conservation in arid and industrial areas. (3 marks)

Model answer

In arid areas: afforestation, proper management of grazing, planting shelter belts of plants, control on overgrazing and stabilisation of sand dunes by growing thorny bushes. In industrial and suburban areas: proper management of waste lands, control of mining activities, and proper discharge and disposal of industrial effluents and wastes after treatment.

11.

Explain the factors responsible for the formation of soil. (3 marks)

Model answer

Relief, parent rock or bedrock, climate, vegetation and other forms of life, and time are important factors. Forces of nature — change in temperature, running water, wind, glaciers and the activities of decomposers — contribute, and chemical and organic changes in the soil are equally important. Soil consists of organic (humus) and inorganic materials and takes millions of years to form a few centimetres deep.

12.

Compare alluvial soil and black soil. (5 marks)

Model answer

Alluvial: most widely spread; deposited by the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra in the northern plains, and found in the eastern coastal deltas; consists of sand, silt and clay; classified as bangar (old, more kanker, more fine particles) and khadar (new, more fertile); rich in potash, phosphoric acid and lime; grows sugarcane, paddy, wheat and pulses; intensively cultivated and densely populated. Black: also called regur or black cotton soil; formed from the Deccan trap basalt lava flows; covers Maharashtra, Saurashtra, Malwa, Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh; clayey, holds moisture, rich in calcium carbonate, magnesium, potash and lime but poor in phosphoric contents; develops deep cracks in hot weather which aerates the soil; sticky when wet; ideal for cotton.

13.

Why is laterite soil not very fertile, and where is it useful? (3 marks)

Model answer

Laterite soil forms under tropical and subtropical climates with alternate wet and dry seasons and is the result of intense leaching due to heavy rain, which removes nutrients; it is acidic (pH < 6.0) and generally deficient in plant nutrients, and is prone to erosion because of its position on the landscape. With appropriate soil conservation techniques, particularly in the hilly areas of Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu, it is very useful for growing tea and coffee; red laterite soils of Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and Kerala suit cashew nut.

14.

Distinguish between gully erosion and sheet erosion. (2 marks)

Model answer

Gully erosion: running water cuts through clayey soil and makes deep channels called gullies; the land becomes unfit for cultivation and is called bad land (ravines in the Chambal basin). Sheet erosion: water flows as a sheet over a large area down a slope and washes away the top soil.

15.

Explain any four methods of soil conservation. (4 marks)

Model answer

(i) Contour ploughing — ploughing along contour lines decelerates the flow of water down slopes. (ii) Terrace cultivation — steps cut on slopes restrict erosion; well developed in the western and central Himalayas. (iii) Strip cropping — large fields divided into strips with strips of grass between crops, breaking the force of the wind. (iv) Shelter belts — rows of trees planted to create shelter, which stabilise sand dunes and the desert in western India.

10

Previous Year Questions (PYQs)

Asked in CBSE board exams

Previous year questions

These follow the pattern of questions set in CBSE Social Science papers for this chapter. Answers are model answers.

1.
CBSE pattern

“Resources are a function of human activities.” Justify the statement. (CBSE pattern, 3 marks)

Model answer

Resources are not free gifts of nature. Human beings transform material available in the environment into resources and use them, through technology and institutions. A substance becomes a resource only when it is technologically accessible, economically feasible and culturally acceptable — for example, petroleum was not a resource until drilling and refining technology existed. Human beings are therefore themselves essential components of resources.

2.
CBSE pattern

State the differences between potential and developed resources with examples. (2 marks)

Model answer

Potential resources are those found in a region but not yet utilised, e.g. solar and wind energy in Rajasthan and Gujarat. Developed resources are those surveyed and whose quantity and quality have been determined for use, e.g. petroleum and natural gas in Bombay High.

3.
CBSE pattern

Why is resource planning necessary in India? Give any three reasons. (3 marks)

Model answer

(i) Resources are unevenly distributed — some regions are rich in certain resources and deficient in others (Jharkhand has minerals but Arunachal Pradesh has water while lacking infrastructure; Rajasthan has solar and wind energy but lacks water). (ii) Irrational consumption and over-utilisation have caused depletion and ecological crises, so judicious use is needed. (iii) Balanced planning at national, state, regional and local levels is required so that all regions develop and resources are conserved for future generations.

4.
CBSE pattern

Explain the contribution of the Brundtland Commission Report. (2 marks)

Model answer

The Brundtland Commission Report of 1987 made the seminal contribution to resource conservation at the global level. It introduced the concept of “sustainable development” and advocated it as a means for resource conservation; it was subsequently published as the book Our Common Future.

5.
CBSE pattern

Define net sown area and gross cropped area. (2 marks)

Model answer

Net sown area is the physical extent of land on which crops are sown and harvested. Gross cropped area is the area sown more than once in an agricultural year plus the net sown area.

6.
CBSE pattern

“Land is an asset of finite magnitude.” Explain the statement with reference to India. (3 marks)

Model answer

Land cannot be increased: India’s total geographical area is fixed at 3.28 million sq km. Competing uses — agriculture, forests, settlements, roads, industry — all draw on the same land, so an increase in one reduces another. Net sown area and forest have therefore changed only marginally between 1960–61 and 2019–20, and forest remains far below the desired 33 per cent. Careful planning is essential because land supports natural vegetation, wildlife, human life, economic activity, transport and communication.

7.
CBSE pattern

Why is black soil good for cotton? Give three reasons. (3 marks)

Model answer

(i) It is made of extremely fine clayey material and has a high capacity to hold moisture, which suits cotton. (ii) It is rich in calcium carbonate, magnesium, potash and lime. (iii) It develops deep cracks in hot weather, which aerates the soil. It is formed from the lava flows of the Deccan trap and is also called black cotton soil.

8.
CBSE pattern

Mention any three characteristics of arid soil. (3 marks)

Model answer

(i) It ranges from red to brown in colour, is sandy in texture and saline in nature; in some areas salt is obtained by evaporating water. (ii) It lacks humus and moisture because of the dry climate, high temperature and faster evaporation. (iii) The lower horizons contain kankar due to increasing calcium content downwards, and the kankar layer restricts infiltration of water; after proper irrigation it becomes cultivable, as in western Rajasthan.

9.
CBSE pattern

How does mining cause land degradation? (2 marks)

Model answer

Mining sites are abandoned after excavation is complete, leaving deep scars and traces of over-burdening. In states like Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh and Odisha, deforestation due to mining has caused severe land degradation.

10.
CBSE pattern

Explain the importance of the National Forest Policy, 1952, in the context of land use. (2 marks)

Model answer

The National Forest Policy (1952) outlined that forest should cover 33 per cent of the geographical area, which was considered essential for maintaining ecological balance. Actual forest cover (23.41 per cent in 2019–20) is far lower than this desired level.

11

Frequently Asked Questions

Quick clarifications

1.

Is a resource the same as a natural endowment?

Model answer

No. A natural endowment becomes a resource only when it is technologically accessible, economically feasible and culturally acceptable. Petroleum lying under the sea was not a resource before drilling technology existed.

2.

What is the difference between bangar and khadar?

Model answer

Bangar is old alluvial soil with a higher concentration of kanker nodules and more fine particles; khadar is new alluvial soil and is more fertile than bangar.

3.

Why does black soil develop cracks?

Model answer

Because it is made of extremely fine clayey material, it shrinks and cracks deeply during hot weather. The cracks help in proper aeration of the soil.

4.

Why is laterite soil acidic?

Model answer

Intense leaching by heavy rain in tropical and subtropical climates with alternate wet and dry seasons removes bases from the soil, leaving it acidic with a pH below 6.0 and deficient in plant nutrients.

5.

Do I need to memorise the percentages in Fig. 1.4?

Model answer

Learn the main ones: net sown area about 45.6 per cent and forest about 23.4 per cent in 2019–20, and that the change since 1960–61 is marginal. For answers, the more useful figures are 33 per cent (forest target), 93 per cent (land use reporting), 3.28 million sq km (area) and 95 per cent (basic needs from land).

6.

Which soil is called regur soil?

Model answer

Black soil, formed from the lava flows of the Deccan trap; it is ideal for cotton and is also called black cotton soil.

7.

Is terrace cultivation the same as contour ploughing?

Model answer

No. Contour ploughing means ploughing along contour lines so water does not run straight down a slope. Terrace cultivation means cutting steps into the slope itself. Both reduce soil erosion, and they are often used together.

8.

Why is the land under forest not increasing much?

Model answer

Because land is finite and under pressure from agriculture, settlements, industry and infrastructure; the same land cannot be both forest and field. Hence forest area grows only marginally and remains below the 33 per cent target.

12

Assertion-Reason Questions

Choose the correct option

How to answer

(a) Both A and R are true and R explains A. (b) Both are true but R does not explain A. (c) A is true, R is false. (d) A is false, R is true.

1.

Assertion (A): Resources are not free gifts of nature.
Reason (R): Resources are a function of human activities; human beings transform material in the environment into resources.

2.

Assertion (A): Resource planning is essential in India.
Reason (R): India has enormous diversity in the availability of resources, with some regions rich in one resource and deficient in another.

3.

Assertion (A): Sustainable development means development in the present should not compromise the needs of future generations.
Reason (R): Sustainable existence is a component of sustainable development.

4.

Assertion (A): About 43 per cent of India’s land area is plain.
Reason (R): Plains provide facilities for agriculture and industry.

5.

Assertion (A): Laterite soil is very fertile and needs no treatment.
Reason (R): Laterite soil is the result of intense leaching due to heavy rain.

6.

Assertion (A): Over-irrigation causes land degradation in Punjab and Haryana.
Reason (R): Over-irrigation leads to water logging, which increases salinity and alkalinity in the soil.

7.

Assertion (A): Black soil is ideal for growing cotton.
Reason (R): Black soil is rich in phosphoric contents.

8.

Assertion (A): Contour ploughing reduces soil erosion.
Reason (R): Ploughing along contour lines decelerates the flow of water down the slopes.

9.

Assertion (A): The National Forest Policy desired 33 per cent of the geographical area under forest.
Reason (R): Forest area in India is far higher than this desired level.

10.

Assertion (A): Arid soils in western Rajasthan can be made cultivable.
Reason (R): Kankar layers in the lower horizons restrict infiltration of water.

Source-Based and Case-Based Questions

Read the passage or table, then answer

Source 1 — Gandhiji on conservation

Source extract
“There is enough for everybody’s need and not for anybody’s greed.”

Gandhiji placed the greedy and selfish individuals and the exploitative nature of modern technology as the root cause for resource depletion at the global level. He was against mass production and wanted to replace it with production by the masses.

1.

What, according to Gandhiji, is the root cause of resource depletion?

Model answer

Greedy and selfish individuals and the exploitative nature of modern technology.

2.

What did Gandhiji want in place of mass production?

Model answer

Production by the masses.

3.

Which two later works carried this idea forward?

Model answer

Schumacher’s Small is Beautiful (1974), which presented Gandhian philosophy once again, and the Brundtland Commission Report (1987), which introduced sustainable development.

Source 2 — Land use data

Data interpretation
Selected land use categories, 1960–61 and 2019–20 (reporting area = 100%)
Category1960–612019–20
Forest18.11%23.41%
Net sown area45.26%45.64%
Non-agricultural uses4.95%9.06%
Barren and unculturable waste12.01%5.40%

How to read this table: each column is the share of the reporting area in one year. Compare a row across the two columns to see the change.

1.

Which category increased the most between the two years?

Model answer

Area under non-agricultural uses, which nearly doubled from 4.95% to 9.06%.

2.

By how much did forest area increase?

Model answer

From 18.11% to 23.41%, an increase of 5.3 percentage points — still short of the 33% target.

3.

What does the fall in barren and culturable waste land suggest?

Model answer

That waste land has been brought into other uses — cultivation, settlement, roads or industry — which is consistent with the rise in non-agricultural use.

Source 3 — Case study: Rajasthan’s resource paradox

Case study

The state of Rajasthan is very well endowed with solar and wind energy but lacks in water resources. The cold desert of Ladakh is relatively isolated from the rest of the country; it has very rich cultural heritage but is deficient in water, infrastructure and some vital minerals.

1.

What does this case show about the distribution of resources in India?

Model answer

That resources are unevenly distributed: a region may be rich in one resource and acutely short of another.

2.

What kind of planning does such a situation demand?

Model answer

Balanced resource planning at the national, state, regional and local levels.

3.

Name two resources in which Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh are rich.

Model answer

Minerals and coal deposits.

HOTS and Competency-Based Questions

Think beyond the text

Higher order thinking

These ask you to apply, compare or evaluate. Model answers are indicative — your own well-reasoned answer can differ.

1.

A state has abundant rainfall but still faces water scarcity and its soil is being eroded. Using this chapter, explain how both problems could arise and what should be done.

Model answer

Abundant rainfall does not guarantee usable water: much of it may be polluted, or may run off quickly because of deforestation and steep slopes, and unequal access can leave groups without water. Soil erosion follows the same causes — deforestation, overgrazing, construction and mining disturb the balance between soil formation and erosion, and water flowing as a sheet or in gullies washes the top soil away. Remedies: afforestation, contour ploughing, terracing, strip cropping, shelter belts, rainwater harvesting, treatment of effluents and equitable distribution. (Model answer — your own reasoning can differ.)

2.

Why can a resource-rich district remain poor? Answer using the ideas of technology, institutions and human resources.

Model answer

Mere availability does not create development. If the district lacks technology to extract and process its minerals, institutions that can plan and implement projects, and skilled human resources, the resource may be exported as raw material or not used at all. The chapter notes that many resource-rich regions are economically backward while resource-poor regions are developed, and that colonising powers exploited colonies precisely because of their higher technology. Development therefore needs technology, institutional change and quality of human resources along with resources.

3.

Compare the usefulness of alluvial and laterite soils for a farmer, and suggest one conservation measure for each.

Model answer

Alluvial soil is very fertile, rich in potash, phosphoric acid and lime and supports sugarcane, paddy, wheat and pulses; its conservation need is mainly to prevent water logging and salinity (proper irrigation and drainage). Laterite soil is acidic and nutrient-poor but suits tea, coffee and cashew after conservation; it is prone to erosion, so terracing and contour bunding on hilly slopes, along with manuring, are needed.

4.

“Land is a shared inheritance.” Explain the statement and suggest two ways of using land responsibly.

Model answer

We share land with past generations and must share it with future generations too; 95 per cent of our basic needs for food, shelter and clothing come from land, and its extent is fixed. Responsible use means avoiding degradation — controlling overgrazing and mining, treating industrial effluents, using irrigation without water logging — and conserving it through afforestation, shelter belts and proper management of waste land.

5.

The pie charts show forest rising only from 18.11% to 23.41% in six decades. Suggest three practical steps to move closer to 33 per cent and explain the difficulty in each.

Model answer

(i) Afforestation on degraded and culturable waste land — difficult because such land is often of poor quality or already encroached. (ii) Protecting existing forests through community participation such as joint forest management — difficult where livelihoods depend on forest produce. (iii) Preventing the diversion of forest land to roads, mining and industry — difficult because development needs land too. The basic constraint is that land is of finite magnitude.

6.

A student says, “If we have technology, we do not need to conserve resources.” Evaluate this statement.

Model answer

The statement is wrong. Better technology can make low-grade ores usable and improve efficiency, but mineral resources are finite and non-renewable, formed over millions of years, and the rate of replenishment is infinitely small compared with consumption. Technology also increases the scale of extraction and consumption. Conservation through recycling, substitution, improved technologies and judicious use remains essential, along with promoting renewable sources. (Model answer.)

Quick Revision Sheet

One page before the exam

Resource and its classification

  • Resource = technologically accessible + economically feasible + culturally acceptable.
  • Nature, technology and institutions interact; humans transform material into resources.
  • Origin: biotic/abiotic. Exhaustibility: renewable/non-renewable. Ownership: individual, community, national, international. Development: potential, developed, stock/reserves.

Sustainable development and Agenda 21

  • Development without damaging the environment; present must not compromise future needs.
  • Rio Earth Summit, June 1992, more than 100 heads of state; Declaration on Global Climatic Change and Biological Diversity; global Forest Principles; Agenda 21.
  • Agenda 21 → every local government draws its own local Agenda 21.

Resource planning

  • Three steps: inventory → planning structure → matching with national plans.
  • Started with the First Five Year Plan.
  • Resources need technology and institutional change: colonisation example.

Conservation milestones

  • 1968 Club of Rome; 1974 Small is Beautiful; 1987 Brundtland Report (Our Common Future); 1992 Rio.

Land

  • Plains 43%, mountains 30%, plateaus 27%.
  • Total area 3.28 million sq km; data for 93%.
  • Five land use categories; NSA 45.64%, forest 23.41% (2019–20); NSA about 54% with other fallow.
  • Forest target 33% (National Forest Policy, 1952); Punjab and Haryana >80% NSA; four states/UTs <10%.

Land degradation

  • Causes: deforestation, overgrazing, mining and quarrying, over-irrigation (salinity, alkalinity), mineral dust, industrial effluents.
  • Cures: afforestation, grazing management, shelter belts, thorny bushes on dunes, waste land management, treated effluents.

Soils

  • Alluvial: Indus–Ganga–Brahmaputra; bangar (old) and khadar (new); Duars, Chos, Terai.
  • Black/regur: Deccan trap basalt; cotton; holds moisture; poor in phosphoric contents.
  • Red and yellow: crystalline igneous rocks, low rainfall, Deccan east and south.
  • Laterite: “later” = brick; leaching; acidic pH<6.0; tea and coffee after conservation.
  • Arid: red to brown, sandy, saline, kankar layer; western Rajasthan after irrigation.
  • Forest: hilly areas; loamy and silty in valleys, coarse on upper slopes.

Erosion and conservation

  • Gully → bad land/ravines; sheet; wind; wrong ploughing.
  • Contour ploughing, terrace cultivation, strip cropping, shelter belts.
19

Chapter Summary

The whole chapter in a few paragraphs

A resource is anything in our environment that satisfies a need and is technologically accessible, economically feasible and culturally acceptable. Resources arise from the interaction of nature, technology and institutions, and human beings are themselves essential components of resources. They are classified by origin, exhaustibility, ownership and stage of development.

Indiscriminate use has caused depletion, concentration of resources in a few hands and global ecological crises, so equitable distribution and sustainable development are essential. The Rio Earth Summit of 1992 and Agenda 21, the Club of Rome (1968), Schumacher’s Small is Beautiful (1974) and the Brundtland Commission Report (1987) mark the world’s growing concern. India, with its uneven resource distribution, needs balanced resource planning at national, state, regional and local levels, and its planning has three stages, beginning with the First Five Year Plan.

Land is a finite resource. Plains cover 43 per cent of India, mountains 30 per cent and plateaus 27 per cent. Land use is divided into forests, land not available for cultivation, other uncultivated land, fallow land and net sown area; net sown area was 45.64 per cent and forest 23.41 per cent of the reporting area in 2019–20, well below the 33 per cent forest target of 1952. Deforestation, overgrazing, mining, over-irrigation and industrial waste degrade land, and afforestation, shelter belts, dune stabilisation and treated effluents conserve it.

Soil is a living resource formed over millions of years from relief, parent rock, climate, vegetation, life and time. India has alluvial, black, red and yellow, laterite, arid and forest soils, each with its own region and crops. Erosion by water and wind — gully, sheet and wind erosion — is checked by contour ploughing, terrace cultivation, strip cropping and shelter belts.
